dailyBrief.text: Big night ahead, Cleveland: the Guardians face elimination in ALCS Game 6 at Tampa Bay at 8 PM, after Tampa Bay took Sunday's Game 5, 3–1, for a 3–2 series lead. The Browns gave you a walk-off win yesterday — 13–10 over Baltimore and a share of first place — so the city starts the week in a fighting mood. Overnight, Ukraine launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia, setting St. Petersburg oil sites ablaze, while Washington argued over intelligence sharing and the Russia sanctions waiver. Solon woke up clear and frosty at 34°, but it's a sunny, dry day ahead with a high near 67°. Tonight in town: Solon Council votes on the park and trail notes, the Jonas Brothers play Rocket Arena, and the Cleveland Orchestra trio performs at Severance — both shows at 7:30.

weekBrief.text: It's a classic crisp fall week in Solon: dry and sunny almost every day, highs in the mid-to-upper 60s and chilly nights in the 30s — good weather for getting outside and for playoff baseball. The Guardians need two wins in Florida to reach the World Series, with a possible Game 7 Tuesday and the Series itself starting Friday. The Browns take their share of first place to Tennessee on Sunday, the Cavs open at Philadelphia on Thursday and play their home opener Saturday against Brooklyn, and Ohio State gets a bye to heal up at quarterback after Saturday's win at Indiana. Around town: trunk-or-treat Thursday in Solon, Heinen's clam bake Friday in Chagrin Falls, and Barack Obama campaigns in Cleveland on Saturday for the fall races. Grocery play of the week is still Giant Eagle's free-turkey deal — spend $350 by November 8 — and the baby countdown is very much on, so it's a good week to knock a few more checklist items off together.

Trump says Ukraine needs a new negotiator — as U.S. envoys head to Norway for peace talks
items.summary:
The public fight between President Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy escalated again on Monday, even as Washington quietly lined up a fresh round of diplomacy. Speaking to reporters on the South Lawn before a campaign trip to Kansas, Trump said it was time for somebody else to negotiate on Ukraine's behalf and defended Russia's conduct in the war, saying Moscow had, in his words, been fine on Ukraine. Zelenskiy, in a Bloomberg interview, accused the administration of pressuring Kyiv to yield to Russia and said he had offered to stop targeting Russian refineries — a step aimed at diesel prices — in exchange for more Patriot air-defense missiles.

Against that backdrop, Reuters reports that Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and envoy Steve Witkoff are expected to travel to Norway this week for the next round of talks on ending the war, with Zelenskiy expected to attend, according to people familiar with the plans. The schedule is tentative, and the White House did not immediately comment. The dispute has also widened beyond words: Zelenskiy says the speed of Ukraine's Starshield satellite service was reduced by a U.S. policy decision and that intelligence sharing has been limited, claims U.S. officials deny.

The Norway meetings matter because they test whether the argument is a negotiating tactic or a genuine break. Ukraine relies on Starshield, built by SpaceX, for battlefield communications and drone operations, and Ukrainian officials say slower service hampered efforts to intercept Russian strikes. If the talks produce even a framework, the pressure campaign may read as leverage; if they stall, Kyiv faces the prospect of fighting on with a cooler Washington.

Watch for confirmation of the Norway schedule and whether Zelenskiy and the U.S. envoys actually sit down together this week.

items.title: Egypt puts off a vote on backing Saudi Arabia militarily until October 26
items.summary:
Egypt's parliament has delayed until October 26 a vote on whether to authorize the country's armed forces to support Saudi Arabia if Riyadh requests it. Lawmakers adjourned a second closed-door session on Monday that was meant to debate President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi's request, extending a decision that could pull Egypt deeper into the conflict with Yemen's Houthis.

Sisi said on Saturday that Egypt would take any measure necessary to protect its Gulf allies after Houthi attacks on Saudi oil and other infrastructure. Egypt's constitution requires a two-thirds parliamentary majority, after consultation with the National Defence Council, before the military can be sent on a combat mission abroad. The Egyptian Social Democratic Party told its lawmakers to abstain, arguing parliament still lacks basic information about the mission's objectives, scope, duration, cost and risks.

Money hangs over the debate as well. Saudi Arabia has a $5.3 billion deposit at Egypt's central bank due this month, plus about $267 million in interest, which gives Cairo both a reason to stand by Riyadh and a reason to avoid an open-ended commitment while its economy is under pressure. Al-Azhar's grand imam has also called for an urgent Arab and Muslim mediation effort.

The delay keeps Egypt's options open for another week, but the October 26 vote will show how far Cairo is willing to go beyond words.

items.title: U.N. food agency cuts Gaza aid for about 500,000 people over a funding shortfall
items.summary:
The U.N. World Food Programme says funding shortages are forcing it to shrink its Gaza operation, cutting monthly food assistance from a planned 1.6 million people to about 1.1 million. That leaves roughly 500,000 people without the monthly aid the agency had intended to provide.

The need remains severe: about two-thirds of Gaza's population is still acutely food insecure, according to the agency. Briefing coverage put the programme's funding need at roughly $450 million for the next six months and estimated about 1.4 million people in the territory already face crisis-level hunger or worse.

The cut is a reminder that relief in Gaza is now constrained less by logistics alone than by donor money. When a flagship U.N. agency trims its rolls by nearly a third, families who were counted in its plans have to fall back on markets, charities or nothing at all.

What to watch is whether donor governments close the gap in the coming weeks, or whether the smaller caseload becomes the new normal heading into winter.

items.title: Fast-moving grass fire at a Canadian military base kills 4 soldiers and critically injures 19
items.summary:
A grass fire that officials thought was under control turned deadly at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, killing four service members and critically injuring 19 others. Thirty-nine people were hospitalized after the fire, which began on the afternoon of October 17 in a training area, shifted from a smoldering grass fire into a fast-moving blaze pushed by winds reaching about 60 mph.

Prime Minister Mark Carney called it one of the worst tragedies to befall Canadian forces in peacetime and ordered flags on federal buildings lowered to half-staff. Maj. Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of the 1st Canadian Division, said crews knew about the fire for hours but believed it was contained — until the wind shifted and it covered a kilometer in about 36 seconds, a speed he described as abnormal.

The soldiers killed were identified as Sgt. Morgan Wong of the Loyal Edmonton Regiment and Privates Shaun Farrell, Aidan Goulding and Hayden Lykkemark of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry.

Investigators will now focus on how a monitored training-area fire was judged safe hours before it turned fatal — a question with implications for every base that trains in dry, windy country.

items.title: The Louvre stays shut on Monday as protesters barricade its entrances in Paris
items.summary:
Visitors who arrived at the Louvre on Monday morning found the world's most-visited museum closed, its glass pyramid and the Carrousel du Louvre and Passage Richelieu entrances barricaded by protesters. The museum posted a notice blaming student strikes and apologizing for the inconvenience, according to Le Monde, and no reopening time was announced.

The blockade was organized by students from the École du Louvre in solidarity with the nationwide protest movement over the cost of living and recent police actions — the same unrest that produced a weekend of riots, looting and thousands of arrests across France. On a busy day the Louvre can draw up to 20,000 visitors, so a full-day closure is both a logistical headache and a loud symbolic statement.

That symbolism is the point. Shutting a global landmark extends the protests beyond the streets and into France's cultural and tourism economy, keeping the pressure on the government even on a day when the rioting itself had subsided.

Watch whether the museum reopens Tuesday and whether other landmarks or universities join the barricade tactic this week.

items.title: French markets tumble as the riots deepen the government's budget headache
items.summary:
Investors marked France down sharply on Monday as the weekend's unrest collided with the country's already difficult finances. French bonds, Paris-listed stocks and the euro all fell, with France's 10-year yield jumping 13 basis points to 4.9% — on track for its biggest one-day rise since late September — and the gap over Germany's benchmark yield widening to 146 basis points, the highest in two weeks.

The government spent the day trying to restore order and confidence at once. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu asked local authorities to impose partial curfews this evening, said a state of emergency remained an option if needed, and ruled out putting all of Paris under curfew. Mayors of the biggest cities, meanwhile, demanded answers over what they called inadequate preparation, and several European governments warned their citizens in France to avoid crowds.

The market move matters because it prices the politics directly into France's borrowing costs. A government already struggling to cut a large deficit now faces riot damage, compensation demands and a higher interest bill at the same time, six months before a presidential election.

What to watch is whether calm holds through the week — another violent weekend would likely push yields closer to the 4.99% level last seen, before this month, in 2002.

items.title: Appeals court blocks the Trump administration from overhauling fair-housing grants
items.summary:
A federal appeals court in Boston refused on Monday to let the Trump administration proceed with its overhaul of the Fair Housing Initiatives Program, the 1987 program that funds nonprofits which prevent and investigate housing discrimination. The ruling largely keeps in place a lower-court order blocking the changes while the case continues.

The administration had planned to steer $46 million of the $56 million Congress appropriated into just five grants — including $25 million to a single law school — instead of the program's usual pattern of more than 100 grants ranging from $75,000 to $425,000. Its plan also attached conditions barring funded work tied to what it called gender ideology or illegal immigration. The National Fair Housing Alliance and the Massachusetts Fair Housing Center sued in July.

The three-judge panel, all Democratic appointees, said the administration had not shown that District Judge Myong Joun exceeded his authority. The court lifted only the part of the order dealing with expired fiscal 2025 funding notices, after Congress extended that money's availability to September 30, 2027.

For the nonprofits that test landlords and investigate complaints, the ruling preserves the existing system for now — and adds one more courtroom loss to the administration's running fight over redirecting congressionally approved spending.

items.title: Trump names two more judge picks as the Senate plans a post-midterm confirmation push
items.summary:
President Trump announced two more nominees for lifetime seats on the federal bench on Monday, both of them Justice Department lawyers. Eric Hamilton, a deputy assistant attorney general and former Nebraska solicitor general, was nominated for a district court seat in Nebraska, and Joseph Falvey, a federal prosecutor who once clerked for Chief Justice John Roberts, was nominated for the Northern District of Indiana.

Trump praised Hamilton for work defending the administration's tariffs, its effort to curtail birthright citizenship, National Guard deployments to cities including Los Angeles, and the dismantling of the Department of Education — a résumé that signals the White House is rewarding lawyers who carried its most contested policies.

The nominations set up a busy lame-duck stretch: Senate Judiciary Committee hearings are scheduled for November 10 and 18, after the November 3 midterms, in a push to confirm as many judges as possible before this Congress ends. Since January 2025 the Senate has confirmed 56 Trump judges, 10 of them to appeals courts, against 234 confirmed across his first term.

The stakes are straightforward — every seat filled before January is a seat the next Congress cannot fill differently, whatever happens on Election Day.

items.title: Senator Slotkin's call for 'deterrence' investigations draws a sharp Trump backlash
items.summary:
Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan has ignited a fight inside the midterm campaign with remarks at a University of Chicago event last week. Slotkin said that if Democrats regain Congress they should pursue signature corruption cases against Trump aides who carried out his bidding, not only against Trump himself, so that young graduates weighing jobs in a future administration think twice — in her words, she wants that deterrence message sent.

President Trump responded on Monday by calling Slotkin a low life who is ruining her state and accusing Democrats of running a weaponized government. Sen. Mike Lee accused her of threatening young Americans, and conservative legal activist Mike Davis wrote that she should learn about the Second Amendment — a message Slotkin said amounted to suggesting she be shot, and which she said mobilized death threats against her and her staff.

The exchange captures how the accountability debate has moved beyond Trump personally to the officials around him. Slotkin's argument is that consequences for aides change behavior in the next administration; her critics argue the same idea criminalizes ordinary government service.

With control of Congress two weeks from being decided, the fight gives both parties a preview of how investigations would be framed if Democrats take a chamber.

items.title: Obama calls the federal probe of Rep. Ilhan Omar 'appalling'
items.summary:
Former President Barack Obama has weighed in on the federal investigation of Rep. Ilhan Omar, calling it an appalling use of state power in a lengthy social media post on Sunday that drew fresh coverage and fallout through Monday. Obama wrote that the government cannot selectively target individuals because of their political beliefs, and that the full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official for criticizing the president.

The investigation became public on October 12, when Homeland Security Investigations agents searched Omar's Washington home under a warrant tied to alleged immigration fraud and false statements, and some of her relatives were subpoenaed by the Justice Department. Reporting describes the inquiry as aimed at whether Omar or her relatives lied during her naturalization — a finding that could, in theory, be used to revoke her citizenship and deport her. Omar has called the search the latest step in a campaign of political intimidation and has not been charged.

Obama's intervention raises the profile of a case that sits at the intersection of immigration enforcement and political retaliation claims. A former president accusing the government of targeting a sitting member of Congress is the kind of statement designed to force the administration to defend the probe publicly.

What to watch is whether prosecutors bring charges, produce evidence, or let the investigation sit — each path carries very different political consequences heading into the midterms.

items.title: The midterms are on track to be the most expensive ever, topping $15 billion raised
items.summary:
The 2026 midterms are on pace to be the most expensive in American history, with more than $15 billion raised to influence control of Congress, according to NPR's analysis of the last major campaign finance filings before Election Day.

The single largest force is Elon Musk, who has spent more than a quarter-billion dollars in recent months: $158 million to the Republican Senate super PAC, $89 million to his own America PAC, $20 million to a Republican House super PAC and $10 million to a pro-Ken Paxton super PAC in Texas. That $158 million Senate contribution alone exceeds what the Texas Senate campaigns of Paxton and Democrat James Talarico raised combined — Talarico reported more than $60 million from July through September.

Below the mega-donor level, Democrats outraised Republicans in about four of five Senate races last quarter, and in the 13 races rated competitive by the Cook Political Report, Republicans were outraised roughly five to one. About three-quarters of planned ad spending through Election Day sits in races favoring Republicans or rated toss-ups.

The money picture explains the air war voters are seeing: record fundraising does not mean an even fight everywhere, but a small set of Senate races absorbing historic sums from both parties — and from one donor in particular.

items.title: 2028 Democratic rivals are using the Texas governor's race to undercut Andy Beshear
items.summary:
An early fight in the 2028 Democratic presidential primary is playing out through the Texas governor's race. Axios reports that Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who heads the Democratic Governors Association, is in open war with prominent Latino lawmakers over the association's spending choices.

Latino leaders have pressed Beshear to invest heavily in Gina Hinojosa's campaign against Gov. Greg Abbott in Texas, and he has resisted, preferring to concentrate the group's money in other states. Meanwhile three potential 2028 rivals — Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, California Gov. Gavin Newsom and Maryland Gov. Wes Moore — have each given money to Hinojosa's bid and earned praise from the same Latino lawmakers pressing Beshear.

The dispute matters beyond one race because it is really about Democrats' slide with Latino voters, one of the party's most urgent problems. Whoever is seen as the governor who took that problem seriously — or who ignored it — carries that reputation into 2028.

Texas was always a long shot for Democrats, which is exactly why the argument is about signals and relationships rather than a realistic path to the governor's mansion this year.

items.title: Tech stocks rebound at Monday's close — Nasdaq jumps 1.1%, the Dow slips
items.summary:
Wall Street's Monday session ended with a tech-led rebound from last week's AI selloff. The Nasdaq Composite climbed 1.11% to close at 26,430.89, the S&P 500 rose 0.41% to 7,690.73, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average eased 0.07% to 51,966.03.

Memory and storage stocks did the heavy lifting: Western Digital gained about 6%, SanDisk roughly 5.5%, Seagate about 3.4% and Micron about 3%, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index added 1.61% with 26 of its 30 stocks higher. The bounce followed a rough Friday, when the Nasdaq fell 2.15% and the S&P 500 lost 1.09%.

Underneath the headline gains, the rally was narrow — only about 176 of the S&P 500's stocks advanced in late trading, and technology was the only sector with a clearly positive average return. The 10-year Treasury yield rose to about 5.15% and Brent crude held near $109 a barrel, both reminders that the financing backdrop for the AI buildout is still expensive.

The week now turns to earnings, with Meta, Tesla, Netflix and SpaceX all reporting — results that will decide whether Monday was a genuine reset or just a pause in the selloff.

items.title: Anthropic pledges 5% of its shares — roughly $48 billion — to a public benefit fund
items.summary:
Anthropic says it plans to set aside 5% of its equity for a new public-benefit fund, a stake worth about $48 billion at the company's last reported valuation. The plan still needs shareholder approval.

The company was valued at roughly $965 billion in a May funding round that raised $65 billion, and it is reportedly preparing for a possible November initial public offering that could seek a valuation near $1.5 trillion. Under the structure, the board could add another 2% of equity for every 50% increase in valuation above an undisclosed benchmark, and the fund could support nonprofits, direct distributions and work on the economic and social effects of AI.

Anthropic has already committed $200 million to efforts addressing AI-related labor disruption, and as a public benefit corporation its directors are required to weigh the public interest alongside shareholder returns. A pledge of this size turns that legal structure into a concrete financial claim.

If the IPO prices anywhere near the reported range, the fund would instantly become one of the largest philanthropic pools in the tech industry — and a test of whether benefit-corporation promises survive contact with public markets.

items.title: Homeland Security orders DeepSeek removed from all civilian federal systems
items.summary:
The Department of Homeland Security has ordered every civilian federal agency to remove DeepSeek products — and any third-party services built on its models — from their systems, and has barred future purchases of the Chinese AI tools.

The order, issued under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018 and posted for publication in the Federal Register, covers departments including State, Treasury and Justice, while excluding defense agencies. Summaries of the action say the ban took effect at the end of July and became public on Monday. Officials cited the risk of sensitive data being transferred to China, the possibility of the models generating actionable intelligence on U.S. persons and agencies, and potential malware or security weaknesses.

Several agencies, including Commerce and the Navy, and a number of states had already imposed narrower DeepSeek restrictions. Monday's order turns those patchwork bans into a government-wide civilian rule.

The move is the latest step in a widening U.S. effort to keep Chinese AI systems out of official infrastructure, and it puts pressure on vendors whose products quietly incorporate third-party models to prove what is running under the hood.

items.title: SoftBank is in early talks to buy security giant Allied Universal in a deal that could reach $18 billion
items.summary:
SoftBank Group is in early-stage talks to acquire Allied Universal, one of the world's largest private-security companies, from Warburg Pincus and the Canadian pension fund La Caisse, according to The Wall Street Journal. A deal is far from certain, but if it happens it could value Allied at as much as $18 billion, excluding debt.

Allied operates in more than 100 countries and territories and generates about $23 billion in annual revenue, much of it from the unglamorous work of staffing guards at offices, warehouses, hospitals and events. SoftBank shares fell about 2% in Tokyo on the report.

The logic is SoftBank's all-in turn toward AI and automation: the company has put $64 billion into OpenAI, is planning data centers, owns Arm, and last year agreed to buy ABB's industrial robotics business for $5.4 billion. A global security workforce is, among other things, one of the largest potential markets for patrol robots and AI monitoring.

For now this is a talks-stage story, but it shows how far SoftBank's buying spree has moved beyond software into the physical economy.

items.title: AI chip challenger Tenstorrent raises $1.5 billion at a $6.2 billion valuation
items.summary:
Tenstorrent, the Santa Clara chip startup trying to build an alternative to Nvidia's AI hardware, said Monday it has raised $1.5 billion in a late-stage funding round that values the company at $6.2 billion — more than double its December 2024 valuation.

The round was led by Trace Capital and Innovation X, with backing from Cathie Wood's ARK Invest, SanDisk, Morgan Stanley, T. Rowe Price and Tether Investments. The money will go toward scaling production of its Galaxy servers, which combine dozens of Tenstorrent chips into systems for chatbots, coding assistants and video generators.

The company's pitch is openness: its chips and software are built on RISC-V, the open-source architecture, rather than a proprietary stack. Its chief executive, Jim Keller, is a well-known chip designer who previously led Tesla's self-driving chip effort and held senior design roles at Apple and AMD. Its previous round, in December 2024, raised more than $693 million at a $2 billion pre-money valuation.

A $1.5 billion raise in a market jittery about AI financing shows investors are still willing to fund credible challengers — especially ones selling the picks and shovels rather than the models.

items.title: SpaceX reports earnings on Tuesday, with Wall Street expecting about $12.7 billion in revenue
items.summary:
Elon Musk's SpaceX steps into the earnings spotlight on Tuesday, in one of the most closely watched reports of the week. Consensus estimates center on about $12.7 billion in revenue and earnings of 14 cents a share.

The report lands in a noisy moment for the company: a public row over interrupted Starlink service to Ukraine, speculation about a possible combination with Musk's Tesla — which also reports this week — and broader market jitters about how AI infrastructure spending is being financed. At about $146, the SpaceX share price sits roughly 8% above its June IPO price, while Wall Street's median 12-month price target is $221.

That gap between the current price and the target is the story: analysts still see large upside, but the stock has to prove its growth can keep pace with a valuation built on launch dominance, Starlink subscriptions and government contracts.

Tesla's report later this week means Musk's two public companies will effectively be graded back to back — a rare double test of the premium investors put on his empire.

items.title: Homebuilder sentiment falls to its lowest since 2012 as mortgage rates reach 7.40%
items.summary:
America's homebuilders are as gloomy as they have been in more than a decade. The NAHB/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index dropped three points in October to 29, its lowest reading since June 2012 and below the 31 economists had forecast.

The backdrop is borrowing cost: the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate hit 7.40% last week, the highest in nearly three years, and it is squeezing buyers out of the market. The gauge of buyer traffic fell five points to 18, its lowest since April 2012 outside the pandemic shock, and 43% of builders said they cut prices in October, by an average of 6%.

Builders also flagged a newer pressure: NAHB chairman Bill Owens said more than a third of builders reported immigration enforcement activity in their market areas over the past month, causing construction delays — a labor problem layered on top of a rates problem.

Housing was already the economy's weak spot; a sentiment reading in the 20s says builders expect it to stay that way until mortgage rates come down in a meaningful way.

items.title: Ukrainians and Sudanese can keep temporary protected status for now, DHS says on the day it was set to expire
items.summary:
The Department of Homeland Security said on Monday — the very day their protections had been scheduled to expire — that immigrants from Ukraine and Sudan can keep Temporary Protected Status for now, with formal announcements to come at the appropriate time.

About 240,000 Ukrainians who fled Russia's invasion have registered for TPS in the United States, and an estimated 6,800 holders come from Sudan, where a war between the army and a rival paramilitary force has produced a major humanitarian crisis. TPS shields holders from deportation and allows them to work legally.

The reprieve is the second in as many months: in September the administration allowed Salvadoran TPS holders to keep their protections too. That sits alongside moves to revoke TPS for people from Haiti, Venezuela, Somalia, Yemen, Syria and other countries, making the program a patchwork decided nationality by nationality.

For the families affected, Monday's statement removes an immediate cliff edge — but 'for now' leaves the longer-term question unanswered, and employers and schools still cannot plan far ahead.

items.title: Trump signs an order creating a new NIH women's health division and a White House task force
items.summary:
President Trump signed an executive order in the Rose Garden on Monday creating a Women's Health Division inside the National Institutes of Health and a White House Women's Health Task Force, the result of a push led by First Lady Melania Trump.

The task force will be led by White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles — who recently announced she is free of breast cancer — together with Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The new division must be set up inside an appropriate NIH institute or center within 90 days, and it will not replace the NIH Office of Research on Women's Health, which has existed since 1990.

The order emphasizes midlife conditions including osteoporosis, Alzheimer's disease, heart disease and stroke, along with maternal health, mental health and endometriosis. The NIH currently spends about $5 billion a year on women's health, roughly 10% of its budget, and the White House did not announce new funding alongside the order.

The test will be whether a new division and task force change research priorities in practice, or mainly reorganize the offices that already do this work.

items.title: Justice Department charges 28 foreign nationals in California with illegal voting and registration crimes
items.summary:
The Justice Department announced Monday that it has charged 28 foreign nationals in California — all of them green card holders, according to the U.S. Attorney for the Central District — with combinations of unlawful voting by an alien, falsely claiming U.S. citizenship to vote or register, and depriving Californians of a fair election.

Eleven of the 28 are in custody, with the rest expected to be taken into custody soon, First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said. Nationwide, the department says it has now charged 113 people with illegal voting or registration offenses. The California cases come from a list of 20,000 people the department told state officials last week it believes are likely noncitizens registered to vote in the state, as part of an effort it calls Operation Protect the Vote, coordinated by California's four U.S. attorneys. Some of those charged are alleged to have voted in the 2024 general election.

California Secretary of State Shirley Weber pushed back, saying she will not disenfranchise thousands of voters based on an unsupported and likely inaccurate belief, noting that ballots are already delivered and early voting for the midterms is underway in a state with more than 23 million registered voters.

The clash sets up a familiar fight — federal prosecutors presenting individual criminal cases while state officials warn against mass challenges to the rolls this close to an election.

items.title: Powder-letter scare spreads, as Rep. Mark Pocan's Madison office becomes the latest target
items.summary:
A staffer in U.S. Rep. Mark Pocan's district office in Madison recognized a suspicious piece of mail on Monday afternoon and did not open it — the latest in a nationwide series of mailings containing an unidentified powdery substance. A Madison Fire Department hazmat crew responded to the office near the Wisconsin Capitol, and the item was sent for testing.

The pattern has been building for days: Rep. Gwen Moore's Milwaukee office received similar mail, confirmed October 16, and the Wisconsin Elections Commission got a similar piece on October 14. The FBI and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating mailings sent to congressional offices, secretaries of state and election offices around the country, including in Oklahoma, Louisiana and Ohio, with targets named so far including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Sens. Kristen Gillibrand, Chris Murphy and Lisa Blunt Rochester.

Whether the powder proves harmful or a hoax, the effect is the same: district offices and election administrators have to treat routine mail as a hazard in the middle of early voting. Pocan said House Democrats have a security call planned for Tuesday to discuss the mailings.

Investigators have not announced a suspect or a motive, so offices are working on pattern recognition alone — exactly what Pocan's staffer did.

items.title: Nestlé will close its Solon factory by the end of 2027, moving production to South Carolina
items.summary:
Nestlé told employees at its Solon factory on Monday that the plant will close by the end of 2027. The Solon site is one of seven Nestlé facilities in Ohio, and the closure will affect hundreds of positions, though the company has not confirmed an exact number of jobs.

Production of Nestlé Professional Solutions pouches will gradually move to the company's Gaffney, South Carolina location over the coming months. The closure applies only to the Solon factory itself — the broader Solon campus will remain open, and Nestlé's Streetsboro distribution center and its West 25th Street factory in Cleveland will not be affected.

For Solon, this is a slow-motion blow rather than a sudden one: a major food-manufacturing employer is winding down over roughly a year, which gives workers time to plan but also means a long stretch of uncertainty about which roles move, which end early and what replaces the plant on the site.

Watch for the city and the company to put numbers on the job losses, and for any discussion of what happens to the factory property once production leaves.

items.title: Guardians set their Game 6 lineup for tonight's elimination game — and save Gavin Williams for a possible Game 7
items.summary:
The Guardians' season comes down to tonight in St. Petersburg: Game 6 of the ALCS against Tampa Bay starts at 8:08 PM ET at Tropicana Field on TBS, with the Rays leading the series 3-2 after Sunday's 3-1 win in Game 5. Cleveland has posted its lineup — Steven Kwan leads off in left, followed by José Ramírez, Chase DeLauter, Jo Adell, Nathaniel Lowe, Travis Bazzana, Patrick Bailey, Petey Halpin and Brayan Rocchio.

On the mound, reliever Shawn Armstrong (2-1, 4.58 ERA) opens a bullpen game for Cleveland against Tampa Bay's Freddy Peralta (10-11, 4.42 ERA), who threw six scoreless innings against the Guardians in Game 2. The deliberate choice by manager Stephen Vogt is who is not pitching: ace Gavin Williams will not start on short rest, because the club wants him fully ready if the series reaches a Game 7 on Tuesday.

Tampa Bay's Yandy Díaz has been the series' quiet problem for Cleveland, with 8 hits in 23 at-bats, and the Rays are chasing their third World Series appearance after 2008 and 2020. Milwaukee, which swept the NLCS, awaits the winner.

It is a classic elimination-game bet: survive tonight with the bullpen, and tomorrow the Guardians get their ace with everything on the line.

items.title: Cleveland-Cliffs stock jumps 15.7% on its strongest quarter in three years
items.summary:
Cleveland-Cliffs delivered the kind of quarter it has been promising for years, and the market noticed: shares surged 15.7% on Monday after the Cleveland steelmaker reported its strongest quarter in three years, well ahead of the roughly 10% jump seen earlier in the day.

Third-quarter revenue was $5.61 billion, up from $4.73 billion a year earlier, with steel shipments of 4.2 million net tons at an average selling price of $1,177 per ton, up from $1,032. Adjusted EBITDA of $612 million beat the company's own $575 million guidance, and net income was $165 million, or 26 cents a share, against a loss of $251 million a year ago. The company guided fourth-quarter adjusted EBITDA to about $715 million.

Chief executive Lourenco Goncalves credited the administration's trade policy for what he called the best price environment in three years, forecast 2027 adjusted EBITDA above $4 billion, and blamed Canada's government for planned layoffs of hundreds of workers at the Stelco operations in Ontario, including an idled Hamilton galvanizing line.

For Northeast Ohio, Cliffs is a bellwether: when its order book and prices run hot, the region's steel supply chain — and a lot of local paychecks — tend to feel it.

items.title: Acton's campaign attacks Ramaswamy over his New York attorney registration — a claim, not a ruling
items.summary:
The Ohio governor's race took a legalistic turn on Monday, when Dr. Amy Acton's campaign accused Vivek Ramaswamy of violating New York's attorney registration rules. This is a campaign allegation, not a finding by any court or regulator, and it is worth reading in that light.

The campaign's claim rests on addresses: it says that in July 2026 Ramaswamy listed a West Chester, Ohio residence as his home address on his New York State attorney registration, while his Ohio voter registration, filed in 2021, uses a Columbus residence. New York's rules require attorneys to list their home address and to amend the filing within 30 days of any change, with noncompliance open to disciplinary action.

From there the campaign argues a fork: either the New York filing breaches registration rules, or, if West Chester is his real home, his Columbus voter registration violates Ohio law — which it characterizes as a fifth-degree felony. No independent adjudication of either claim was reported with the release.

Expect the Ramaswamy campaign to answer with its own reading of the filings; until a regulator or court weighs in, this is best filed under hardball campaign lawyering rather than established misconduct.

items.title: Ohio State's trip to USC is set for 7:30 PM on NBC on October 31, as the bye week arrives
items.summary:
The Big Ten announced on Monday that Ohio State's game at USC on Saturday, October 31 will kick off at 7:30 PM ET on NBC — the Buckeyes' first NBC game of the season, and a 4:30 PM local start in Los Angeles. It will be Ohio State's first trip to the L.A. Coliseum since 2008, when it lost 35-3; the teams last met in the 2017 Cotton Bowl, a 27-21 Ohio State win.

The timing gives No. 3 Ohio State (6-1) a full bye week — its only one of the regular season — to prepare, and to get its quarterback situation settled. True freshman Luke Fahey, a Southern Californian, is in line to make his first career start at USC after starter Julian Sayin was hurt against Indiana; coach Ryan Day has said Sayin, whose right arm was in a sling after the October 17 game, will probably be out for several weeks.

Ohio State reached the bye with momentum, beating No. 5 Indiana 19-15 on Saturday to climb to No. 3 in the AP poll. USC sits 16th in the AP Top 25.

A freshman quarterback making his first start in the Coliseum, at night, on national television: the bye week will be spent trying to make that sentence sound less dramatic than it is.

items.title: Browns safety Grant Delpit left Sunday's win over Baltimore with a concussion
items.summary:
Cleveland's 13-10 win over the Ravens on Sunday came with a defensive cost: starting safety Grant Delpit was ruled out with a concussion in the first quarter, after going down while tackling Zay Flowers on a jet sweep with 11:21 left in the period.

The Browns offered no postgame update on Delpit's status. He finished with 2 tackles, bringing him to 25 for the season with a sack, an interception and three passes defensed — production that comes with context: he signed a three-year, $45 million extension on July 30 and has been managing a shoulder injury for most of the season.

Rookie Emmanuel McNeil-Warren stepped into Delpit's role and played well, finishing with six tackles, a tackle for loss and a pass defensed, while Daniel Thomas added three tackles as the third safety.

Cleveland, 4-2 and sharing first place in the AFC North, travels to face the 1-5 Titans in Nashville on Sunday, October 25. Whether Delpit clears concussion protocol by then is the defense's main question of the week.
